newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai finance mergers process seen as painful.
newsitem.headline: Thai finance mergers process seen as painful.

text.p: The troubled Thai financial sector will endure more pain to meet a determined push by the central bank for more mergers among the nation's numerous and ailing finance firms, analysts said on Friday.
But despite expected hassles, the process already underway would strengthen the turmoil-ridden sector and prepare it for tougher competition in the future, they told Reuters.
Job losses, difficulty in finding the right partner and frank asset evaluations would be among some of the bullets finance firms would have to bite on their way to a better future.

"It is definitely a right and necessary decision. This is a a loud and clear message from the authorities that those who refuse to shape up will be indirectly forced into extinction," said Supavudh Saichua of Phatra Thanakit, one of Thailand's largest finance and securities companies.
"But getting there might involve some pains along the way," he added.

Supavudh said asset evaluations of firms up for mergers could pose complications. Those with poor-quality assets would need to write off their bad debts before merging and some might even have to sell the shares at huge losses.

This week, the Bank of Thailand, the central bank, sent a clear message to the nation's roughly 90 finance firms -- consolidate or suffer. It even offered bank licences and other sweeteners to foster mergers.
The drive for consolidation follows last month's major revamp by Thai authorities of the finance sector, which has sunk billions of dollars in loans to the troubled property sector.

The central bank ordered 10 weakened finance firms to boost capital and told all financial institutions to raise provisions for poor-quality assets. Analysts believe the problem of non-performing loans among financial institutions is serious.

Since the finance sector shake-up, there have been two mergers already with official blessings. The first last month was a marriage between Thailand's biggest finance firm, Finance One Plc, and medium-sized Thai Danu Bank Plc.
The second merger took place on Thursday between major Thai finance firm Nava Finance and Securities and the smaller CMIC Finance and Thaimex Finance.
Analysts said some finance firms would have to rush to have their assets evaluated soon as the current downturn in the Thai economy could force down the value of their equities.
Although the merger is voluntary, the central bank made it clear that those who cooperated would get business incentives, while those who resisted would be abandoned.
Analysts said the latest central bank stance signalled a monumental policy shift. In the past the central bank bailed out troubled finance firms in order to protect public interest.
During 1978 and 1984, when Thailand faced severe economic downturns, the central bank had to shoulder the hefty burden of resuscitating the finance sector at great expense.
"With the new measures, the Bank of Thailand has reduced the chance to face the same problem again if the next cycle should occur," Supavudh said.
Unemployment in the finance sector could rise as mergers took shape. Those working in corporate lending, funding and the back office would be most vulnerable, analysts said.

"It is almost inevitable that cost cutting and redundancy will lead to job losses. But those who have expertise in specialised areas such as forex or financial instruments might not suffer at all," said an executive at a medium-sized finance firm.

However, an analyst from a major US investment bank said the white-collar unemployment problem would be short-term as the economy is still growing. Those forced out of jobs during the transition could be absorbed by expanded businesses later.

"It's worth going through these pains. (The sector) is already in the mess, no doubt. And this is an appropriate way to get out of it," he said. "If the country does not do this, there will still be uncertainties...the confidence in Thailand will remain bearish."
